content: The provision of comprehensive palliative care involves addressing critical issues such as ensuring equitable access to care, delivering person-centered and respectful care, and fostering community involvement. It also requires informed education on pain and symptom management, as well as psychosocial support. The World Health Organization (WHO), through its Access to Controlled Medicines Programme, supports Member States in reviewing and improving national legislation and policies to strike a balance between preventing the misuse, diversion, and trafficking of controlled substances and ensuring appropriate access to these medicines, in alignment with United Nations international drug control conventions. Efforts are being made to explore ways to increase the availability and accessibility of medicines used in palliative care. This involves consultations with Member States, relevant networks, civil society, and other international stakeholders. Collaboration with the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), health ministries, and other authorities is essential to promote the availability and balanced control of controlled medicines for pain and symptom management. Additionally, the WHO works with the INCB to assist Member States in establishing accurate estimates for the availability of medicines for pain relief and palliative care, including better implementation of guidance on estimating requirements for internationally controlled substances. The WHO also collaborates with UNICEF and other partners to promote and implement palliative care for children. Monitoring the global situation of palliative care and evaluating progress in various initiatives and programs is conducted in partnership with Member States and international organizations. Furthermore, the WHO encourages Member States to allocate adequate funding and improve cooperation for palliative care programs and research, particularly in resource-poor countries, as outlined in the 2014–2015 Programme Budget. Research on effective palliative care models in lowand middle-income countries is also encouraged, with a focus on identifying and applying good practices. The WHO emphasizes the importance of integrating palliative care and symptom relief into pediatric care. Training community health workers (CHWs) is a key component, with a curriculum that includes understanding the medical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs of patients, effective communication, knowing when to seek help, resilience, self-care, and providing grief and bereavement support. These efforts are supported by resources such as the WHO Collaborating Centre for Community Participation in Palliative Care and Long-Term Care in Kerala, India. Palliative care focuses on alleviating serious health-related suffering (SHS) associated with life-limiting or life-threatening conditions or end-of-life care. SHS refers to suffering that cannot be relieved without medical intervention and significantly compromises physical, social, or emotional functioning. The WHO also highlights the importance of addressing social determinants of health, which include the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, as these factors influence health inequities. Universal health coverage (UHC) is a critical goal, ensuring that individuals receive the health services they need without financial hardship. UHC encompasses health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care of sufficient quality to be effective. Integrated health services are designed to provide a continuum of care, addressing health needs throughout an individual’s life course. These services are people-centered, incorporating the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, and empowering them to participate in their own care. Hospice care, as a specialized form of palliative care, provides dedicated inpatient or outpatient services for patients nearing the end of life. Strengthening health systems and fostering intersectoral action are essential to improving health care delivery and quality of life. This involves collaboration across various sectors beyond health to design and implement public policies that address the broader determinants of health.
